The experience of finding out that you are different, and limited, is critical to a healthy sense of self in a person with a developmental disability. It helps them to set standards for themselves that are realistic and to gauge their place in the world. If people around them are supportive and value them as who they are, they'll be happy and successful in life. The vast majority of actually "retarded" people are pretty fun personalities and are enjoyable to spend time with and I don't think this is an unusual point of view. They should and will be protected by those who are able, but that protection is insulting when it denigrates their abilities. They may be limited, but they're not lacking in function - they can understand and reason and handle the criticism that may come from the use of the term "retarded."
